rows.speaker: some

rows.anchor: is read by some as “the winds” that bring the rain clouds

rows.speaker: a small minority
rows.claim: A small minority reads muʿṣirāt as referring to the heavens.
rows.anchor: A small minority read it as a reference to “the heavens”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God remains the primary cause: rain is the means by which He produces grain, plants, and gardens, since He made every living thing from water.
rows.anchor: God remains the primary cause for all things. Therefore, it is not the rain that produces grain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Division is Resurrection, when truth and falsehood, right and wrong, and light and dark are finally distinguished.
rows.anchor: because it provides the ultimate distinction between truth and falsehood, right and wrong, light and dark

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed Moment is guaranteed; God will not fail the tryst.
rows.anchor: It is a Moment Appointed because it is guaranteed, and God will not fail the tryst

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is late Makkan and probably appeared shortly before or after Sūrah 78.
rows.anchor: A late Makkan sūrah, al-Nāziʿāt was most likely revealed shortly before or after Sūrah 78

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is titled from its first word and also called al-Sāhirah after the gathering plain and al-Ṭāmmah after the Great Calamity.
rows.anchor: It is also known as al-Sāhirah

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say the surah directly continues the warning of 78:40, and its focus is the Hour and Resurrection.
rows.anchor: some say that it follows directly upon the first phrase of 78:40

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators say an oath by something displays its greatness, the magnitude of what follows, or both.
rows.anchor: when one makes an oath by a thing, it is to show its greatness or to express the magnitude of what is to follow

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may swear by any created thing, whereas people should swear only by God.
rows.anchor: God may swear an oath by anything He has created, but that it is not proper for human beings to swear by anything other than God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–14 recount disbelievers' questions about Resurrection and reaffirm its attributes.
rows.anchor: Vv. 6–14 recount the questions of those who do not believe in the Resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses and Pharaoh account is likely the earliest revealed account of them and likens Pharaoh's disbelief to that of Makkan idolaters.
rows.anchor: most likely the first account of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in the chronological order of revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wonders of creation are presented as evidence that God can resurrect.
rows.anchor: cite the wonders of creation as evidence of God’s ability to resurrect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 34–41 contrast believers' and disbelievers' outcomes on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: returns to a description of the Day of Resurrection, contrasting the fate of the believers with that of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verses answer disbelievers who taunted the Prophet for not knowing when the Hour would arrive.
rows.anchor: respond to the disbelievers who chided the Prophet for not knowing when the Hour would come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāmmah derives from ṭamma, meaning abundant or rising over, like a flood; its overabundance encompasses everything.
rows.anchor: derives from the verb ṭamma, meaning “to be abundant” or “to rise over,” as would a flood

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some identify the Great Calamity as the trumpet's second cry, gathering all humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: Some take the Great Calamity as a reference to the second cry of the trumpet

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others identify it as Resurrection because it surpasses and predominates over all things.
rows.anchor: others take it as a reference to the Resurrection, because it surpasses and predominates over

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret the Calamity as the moment when Hell's people are led to Hell and Paradise's people to Paradise.
rows.anchor: interpreted by some as a reference to the very moment when the people of Hell are led to Hell

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand the missing response to the conditional as affirming that the event must occur.
rows.anchor: Some view the omission of a response to the conditional when

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone will recall good and evil deeds, including deeds forgotten in worldly life, because all were recorded.
rows.anchor: All people will remember the good and evil that they have done

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maqāma rabbihi means standing before God on Judgment Day and answering for one's deeds; it can also mean the station of one's Lord.
rows.anchor: It indicates being aware of standing before God on the Day of Judgment and answering for all of one’s deeds

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī treats fear of standing before God as the opposite of rebellion: rebellion implies ignorance, while fear implies knowledge.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī sees this fear of standing before his Lord as the exact opposite of one who rebelled in v. 37

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forbidding caprice opposes preferring worldly life; fear of God leads to obedience and good deeds, while caprice leads astray.
rows.anchor: one who forbids the soul from caprice is the opposite of one who prefers the life of this world

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The question is attributed to Makkan idolaters who asked to mock, not to gain information.
rows.anchor: the idolaters of Makkah, who did not ask in order to be informed, but only to mock

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording derives from a nautical metaphor, asking when the Hour will berth.
rows.anchor: derives from a nautical metaphor meaning, “When shall it berth?”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some take the nautical image to imply that the Hour is near.
rows.anchor: Some take the use of this metaphor to imply that it is near at hand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading has God tell the Prophet not to speak about what he does not know.
rows.anchor: God’s telling the Prophet that he is not to speak of that of which he does not know

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading answers people who argued the Prophet had no business mentioning the Hour and its signs without knowing their timing.
rows.anchor: a reference to those who contended that the Prophet had no business mentioning the Hour, its signs, the Resurrection

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet wanted to ask when the Hour would come, but God told him he had no right to know.
rows.anchor: a report from ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet wanted to ask God about the moment when the Hour would come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God knows when the Hour will occur, and He will manifest it at its appointed time.
rows.anchor: Only God knows about the Hour, as in 7:187

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: When Gabriel asked about the Hour, the Prophet answered that the questioned person knows no more than the questioner.
rows.anchor: Regarding that the one questioned knows no more than the questioner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet does not know the Hour or other Unseen matters; his mission is to warn, though prophets also bring glad tidings.
rows.anchor: The Prophet has no knowledge of the Hour and other aspects of the Unseen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People expect prophets to act as soothsayers, but the Prophet follows revelation and is only a clear warner.
rows.anchor: human beings often expect them to function as soothsayers or fortune-tellers

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators say the time in the grave will seem brief before the resurrection and gathering before God.
rows.anchor: Most commentators say that this verse means that the time in the grave will seem short

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say earthly life will seem like only an hour compared with the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Others say the implication is that life on earth will seem as if it were only an hour

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Here morning is said to represent worldly life as people see the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: morning (ḍuḥā) is said to refer to the time period of the worldly life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is an early Makkan surah, also called al-Ṣākhkhah after verse 33 and al-Safarah after verse 15.
rows.anchor: an early Makkan sūrah that takes its name from the first sūrah’s word. It is also known as al-Ṣākhkhah

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some connect its opening to 79:45: the Prophet should not focus on indifferent hearers while seekers await guidance.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that it is related to the previous sūrah by the manner in which the first ten verses reinforce the message of 79:45

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah reports that the passage concerns blind ʿAbd Allāh ibn Umm Maktūm, who repeatedly sought guidance while the Prophet addressed Makkan leaders; the Prophet turned away, and the verses rebuked him.
rows.anchor: ʿĀʾishah, the wife of the Prophet, reported that this sūrah was revealed about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Umm Maktūm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Umm Maktūm was among Islam's first converts and devoted to the Prophet and Quran; afterward the Prophet welcomed him as the one for whom his Lord rebuked him.
rows.anchor: After the revelation of this sūrah, it is said that the Prophet would greet him by saying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Umm Maktūm was among the first two migrants to Madinah, taught Quran, and shared the call to prayer with Bilāl.
rows.anchor: Ibn Umm Maktūm was one of the first two people to migrate to Madinah, where he taught the Quran to many people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet sometimes left Madinah in Ibn Umm Maktūm's care; 4:95 is also said to concern his blindness and exemption from campaigns.
rows.anchor: It is also said that 4:95 was revealed regarding the particular case of Ibn Umm Maktūm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though blind and excused from expeditions, Ibn Umm Maktūm insisted on a battlefield role; after Qādisiyyah he was found dead holding the Muslim standard.
rows.anchor: After the Battle of Qādisiyyah in 14/636, he was found dead on the battlefield still clutching the standard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the account of Ibn Umm Maktūm, the surah moves through the angels' book, human ingratitude, divine bounties, and the different Judgment Day outcomes.
rows.anchor: the sūrah alludes to a book written by the angels (vv. 11–16). It then transitions into a discussion of humanity’s ingratitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgment Day terror will make people care only about themselves; 70:11–14 similarly depicts a person willing to ransom himself with family and all on earth.
rows.anchor: The terror of the Day of Judgment will be so severe that people will not be concerned with anything other than themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic hadith says people will be gathered barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised; a woman asks whether they will see one another naked.
rows.anchor: In a famous ḥadīth, the Prophet said, “People will be gathered barefoot, naked

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet answers the woman's concern by saying each person's own affair will occupy him.
rows.anchor: For every man that Day his affair shall suffice him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This early Makkan surah is probably seventh chronologically, takes its name from the enfolding sun, and is also titled “When the Sun Is Enfolded.”
rows.anchor: is most likely the seventh in the chronological order of revelation

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah links the surah to the previous one because it opens with the Last Day events that conclude it.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah suggests that this sūrah is related to the previous one because it begins by describing the events

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first section describes the Hour and Resurrection through events that invert the apparent order of creation.
rows.anchor: These apocalyptic events are described in a manner that suggests an inversion of the apparent order of the created world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith urges reading the surah to envision Judgment Day as though seeing it, citing its opening signs.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states, “Whosoever wishes to look at the Day of Judgment as if he is seeing it with his own eyes, let him read

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second, more elusive section discusses Quranic revelation through Gabriel and its effect on the human soul.
rows.anchor: The second section of the sūrah is a more elusive passage that discusses the revelation of the Quran through the Archangel Gabriel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAsʿasa can mean either approach or leave, referring to the beginning or end of night, or both.
rows.anchor: which is among a class of Arabic words that can mean either one thing or its very opposite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morning breathes as it seems to awaken from night and its light spreads like exhaled breath until day.
rows.anchor: the manner in which the morning appears to awaken from the night and the way its light expands and spreads like exhaled breath

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: If night approaches in verse 17, this verse refers to morning rising; if night recedes, it refers to morning's rise or gradual illumination.
rows.anchor: If v. 17 is taken as the approach of night, this verse is interpreted to mean “by the morning as it rises”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Chronologically the surah probably follows 82 and is among the last revealed in Makkah; it is named for the sky being rent in its first verse.
rows.anchor: one of the last sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surahs form a progression: 82's angels record deeds, 83 contrasts the records of wicked and pious, and this surah contrasts those receiving their book in the right hand or from behind.
rows.anchor: Sūrah 82 alludes to the guardian angels who write one’s deeds in a book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah moves from Judgment Day events to contrasting reckonings, then oaths, and finally the different ends of believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with allusions to events that will transpire on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-shafaq is the redness and remaining sunlight after sunset until night, or the interval from sunset until the horizon's last light.
rows.anchor: refers to the remaining redness and light of the sun after its setting at the beginning of the night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasaqa conveys gathering together like a herd; night symbolically gathers all in darkness as all will ultimately return to God.
rows.anchor: conveys the notion of “gathering together (in one herd)” and points to the symbolic power of night

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators classify al-Fajr as early Makkan, though some call it Madinan; it is probably tenth in revelation order.
rows.anchor: though some maintain that it is Madinan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's opening oaths lead into accounts of tyrants, human vacillation under fortune, rebuke of stinginess, Judgment Day, and the peaceful believing soul.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with a series of oaths (vv. 1–4) followed by brief descriptions of the punishments

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some take the dawn and ten nights as the beginning of Muḥarram and its first ten nights.
rows.anchor: Some see these verses as a reference to the break of dawn at the beginning of Muḥarram

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others identify the dawn with the Feast of Sacrifice and the ten nights with the first ten of Dhu’l-Ḥijjah.
rows.anchor: Others see them as a reference to the break of dawn at the Feast of Sacrifice

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another interpretation points to dawn during Ramadan and its last ten nights, when the Quran was first revealed.
rows.anchor: Others see them as a reference to the break of dawn during Ramadan and the last ten nights of Ramadan

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators understand the verse as night in general, indicating God's wisdom in measuring night and day.
rows.anchor: Most commentators interpret this verse as a reference to night in general

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some take it as the Hajj night when pilgrims gather at Muzdalifah before moving to Minā.
rows.anchor: Some say that it could be a specific reference to the night of the ḥajj

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand it as the Night of Power.
rows.anchor: Others say it could be seen as a reference to the Night of Power

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhī ḥijr derives from ḥajara, “prevent” or “prohibit”; ḥijr can mean intellect because it prevents error and confusion.
rows.anchor: because it prevents one from falling into error and confusion

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Ḥijr can also mean self-control, or ḥilm.
rows.anchor: Ḥijr can also be taken to imply self-control (ḥilm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says Hell will be brought forth with seventy thousand leashes, each pulled by seventy thousand angels.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth says, “Hellfire will be brought forth that Day and it will have seventy thousand leashes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People will remember their conduct, but can no longer repent or make up lost time.
rows.anchor: people will remember how they conducted themselves in this world, but there will be no opportunity for repentance

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators interpret wishing one had sent forth for life as wishing for good deeds that would save one from the Fire.
rows.anchor: Most commentators say Would that I had sent forth for my life means, “Would that I had sent forth good deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says believers too will regret each time they remembered God in life, since that remembrance will be a source of regret on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: even believers will have some regret, since as a ḥadīth says, “There is no time wherein the son of Adam does not remember God

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators consider the surah early Makkan; al-Suyūṭī and others place it immediately after Sūrah 50 in the middle Makkan period, while a minority call it Madinan or partly Madinan.
rows.anchor: although al-Suyūṭī and others maintain that it was revealed immediately after Sūrah 50

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Named for the land in verse 1, the surah opens with oaths and the human condition, then reproaches misuse of faculties and possessions, gives instruction, and contrasts the right and left.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its title from the mention of this land in the first verse. It begins with two oaths

rows.speaker: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets travail as enduring worldly hardships in life and the severities of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: the interpretation attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, “Enduring the hardships of the world in life and the severities of the Hereafter”

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others relate travail to the hardships of worldly life, from birth through death, and say life is toil and trial.
rows.anchor: Others relate it to 46:15, His mother carried him in travail and bore him in travail

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand travail as the trials of death, the grave, and Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: Others see it as a reference to the trials of death, the grave, and the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabad can mean erect or upright; on this reading the verse refers to humans as the only creatures that walk upright on two legs.
rows.anchor: Travail translates kabad, which can also mean “erect” or “upright.” When read this way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says releasing a believing slave will ransom the emancipator from the Fire.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth states, “Whoever releases a believing slave

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: There is debate over whether charity or manumission is more praiseworthy; some consider manumission superior because it comes first here.
rows.anchor: There is a debate as to which is more praiseworthy, charity

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read freeing a neck as freeing oneself through repentance.
rows.anchor: This verse can also imply that one should free one’s own neck

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another reading takes freeing one's neck to mean performing worship to attain Paradise, the greatest freedom.
rows.anchor: by performing the acts of worship by which one attains Paradise, since that is considered to be the greatest freedom

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Giving wealth is harder in times of need but more beneficial; al-Rāzī glosses the verse with the teaching of 2:177 and 76:8.
rows.anchor: giving one’s wealth is more difficult in times of need, though of greater benefit. Thus al-Rāzī glosses this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good works in verses 13–16 must be grounded in belief, the necessary condition for their acceptance.
rows.anchor: One does not assail the steep pass by simply performing the deeds mentioned in vv. 13–16; one must do so on the basis of belief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exhorting to patience means supporting religious practice through hardship and opposition; exhorting to compassion means urging mercy toward God's creatures.
rows.anchor: Exhorting to patience (cf. 103:3) pertains to encouraging one another in maintaining religious practice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says the Merciful shows mercy to the merciful and urges mercy toward people on earth.
rows.anchor: As a famous ḥadīth states,“The merciful are those unto whom the Merciful is merciful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shams is early Makkan and thought to follow Sūrah 97; it takes its title from the opening oath.
rows.anchor: thought by most to have been revealed shortly after Sūrah 97

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first ten verses establish physical and spiritual polarity: eight oaths lead to the soul's choice between iniquity and purity, continuing 90:10's two highways and right-left contrast.
rows.anchor: The first ten verses emphasize the physical and spiritual polarity inherent in creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verses use Thamūd as an example of those destroyed for rejecting and disobeying messengers; its appearance in early and later surahs indicates the story was well known to Arabs.
rows.anchor: The last five verses focus on the story of the northern Arabian tribe Thamūd as an example of what befalls those who reject God’s messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the meaning of ḍuḥāhā, translated “morning brightness,” consult the introduction to Sūrah 93.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of ḍuḥāhā, here translated its morning brightness, see the introduction to Sūrah 93

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read the moon following the sun as an allusion to the moon receiving sunlight.
rows.anchor: This verse can be read as an allusion to the moon’s receiving its light from the sun

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others see the new crescent at the start of each lunar month, appearing near sunset and setting soon after.
rows.anchor: or to the new crescent moon, which at the start of each lunar month is visible above the horizon

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Another reading alludes to the different orbits of sun and moon as measures of time.
rows.anchor: It could also be seen as an allusion to the differing orbits of the moon and the sun

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The day disclosing it may refer to the sun.
rows.anchor: It can be taken as a reference to the sun

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: The referent may instead be the world or earth.
rows.anchor: or to the world or the earth

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: It may refer to darkness, making the sense “by the day when dispersing it.”
rows.anchor: It can also be seen as a reference to “the darkness” (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritually, the verse evokes faith's light extinguishing the darkness of ignorance.
rows.anchor: this verse can be read as an allusion to the light of faith extinguishing the darkness of ignorance

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The night may be understood as enshrouding the sun.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to the night enshrouding the sun

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: The night may instead be understood as enshrouding the world.
rows.anchor: or enshrouding the world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritually, sins that persist cover the light of faith.
rows.anchor: it can be read as an allusion to sins, persistence in which covers the light of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Layl is early Makkan and often considered ninth in revelation order, though some call it Madinan or partly Madinan; it is named after the opening oath.
rows.anchor: often considered the ninth in the chronological order of revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first three verses echo the prior surah's polarity; the rest stresses diverse human ends and the opposed outcomes of good and evil deeds.
rows.anchor: Similar to the first ten verses of the preceding sūrah, the first three verses of this sūrah focus upon the polarity inherent to the created order

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The omitted object of “enshrouds” may be the world.
rows.anchor: The omitted direct object can be seen as an allusion to the world, the earth, the day

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The omitted object may be the earth.
rows.anchor: The omitted direct object can be seen as an allusion to the world, the earth, the day

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The omitted object may be the day.
rows.anchor: The omitted direct object can be seen as an allusion to the world, the earth, the day

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The omitted object may be all of creation.
rows.anchor: The omitted direct object can be seen as an allusion to the world, the earth, the day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse parallels 91:3 and belongs to a recurring sequence of oaths on the alternation of night and day.
rows.anchor: This is one of several passages where an oath is taken by the alternation of night and day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here saʿy means doing or acting: people work either for redemption or perdition, with no in-between.
rows.anchor: implying that people work for either redemption or perdition and that there is no in-between
